subject: Private deployment: recommended transport for BlueCrest pilot (Peering / PrivateLink / S2S)
messages:
From: Alex Johnson <alex.johnson@bluecrest.io>
To: tessa.morgan@redwood.ai
Cc: BlueCrest NetOps <netops@bluecrest.io>
Date: Wed, 12 May 2027 09:08:00 -0700
Subject: Pilot transport question — peering vs PrivateLink vs S2S

Hi Tessa,

Thanks again for the demo last week. We're planning a small pilot with Redwood Private to route requests from our inference clients in our AWS account to Redwood's dedicated VPC. Our NetOps team asked for a short recommendation on which connectivity path to pursue for the pilot: VPC Peering, AWS PrivateLink (interface endpoints), or a site-to-site VPN.

High level constraints:
- Pilot will start with 3 application hosts generating low sustained QPS (~50 requests/sec).
- Data classification: internal PII is out; most payloads are pseudonymized but still sensitive.
- Goal: keep latency sub-60ms p50 to Redwood endpoints.
- Timeline: 3-week pilot, low ops overhead preferred.

Any guidance from your side on tradeoffs (security, latency, operational overhead, scaling to prod) would be super helpful — a short recommendation we can hand to our NetOps folks.

Appreciate it,
Alex
Alex Johnson
Head of Platform Engineering | BlueCrest Analytics
alex.johnson@bluecrest.io
From: tessa.morgan <tessa.morgan@redwood.ai>
To: Alex Johnson <alex.johnson@bluecrest.io>
Cc: karthik.iyer@redwood.ai, marissa.cole@redwood.ai
Date: Wed, 12 May 2027 10:22:00 -0700
Subject: Re: Pilot transport question — peering vs PrivateLink vs S2S

Hi Alex — great question. I've looped in Karthik (network/solutions) and Marissa (eng ops) to make sure we cover both the technical and operational angles. High level recommendation up front: for a short pilot that values low ops overhead and clear security boundaries, start with PrivateLink (interface endpoints).

Why PrivateLink for the pilot (summary):
- Security: provides a clear, managed endpoint in your VPC; traffic never traverses public internet and we can limit access via SGs.
- Low ops: no cross-account route table changes or VPC peering coordination needed; you create and use the inteface endpoint and test immediately.
- Predictable auth surface: we can enforce mTLS and token-based auth at the endpoint level and provision least-privilege SG rules.

Tradeoffs:
- Latency: PrivateLink adds an extra network hop compared to direct peering. For your expected volumes and our benchmarking, p50 should remain <60ms if both sides are in the same region — we will validate during pilot.
- Cost: interface endpoints have per-hour and per-GB costs on the AWS side; small for pilot, material at scale (we can model).
- Scaling: for high-throughput, peering or colocated private tenancy gives better raw throughput; PrivateLink can be sharded across multiple endpoints or subnets if needed.

When Peering or S2S makes sense:
- VPC Peering: preferred when you need the absolute lowest latency and are comfortable with cross-account route propagation and broader surface exposure (peered VPCs can access permitted prefixes). Good for sustained production traffic with committed bandwidth.
- Site-to-site VPN: useful when customers have on-prem data centers and need minimal config changes, or when you want a quick, temporary fallback without cloud-only work. VPNs have higher and more variable latency and are more brittle for high-throughput workloads.

Next steps I propose:
1) We'll validate latency with a quick smoke test using PrivateLink (1–2 days).
2) Share a mutual action plan (MAP) with required subnets/SGs, test tokens, and timeline (attached).
3) If latency or cost becomes a blocker, we'll run a short peering POC and compare.

Karthik — can you add a short technical note on peering implications and any limits we should call out for BlueCrest? Marissa — I'll coordinate the MAP and attach the VPN diagram we discussed.

Thanks,
Tessa Morgan
Customer Solutions | Redwood Inference
From: Karthik Iyer <karthik.iyer@redwood.ai>
To: tessa.morgan <tessa.morgan@redwood.ai>
Cc: Alex Johnson <alex.johnson@bluecrest.io>, marissa.cole@redwood.ai, connor.obrien@redwood.ai
Date: Wed, 12 May 2027 12:15:00 -0700
Subject: Re: Pilot transport question — peering vs PrivateLink vs S2S

Adding technical detail as requested. Long answer short: PrivateLink is the safe default for pilots; peering is the performance option but requires tighter coordination.

Notes on each approach: 
1) AWS PrivateLink (interface endpoints)
- Pros: least blast radius; no route table exchanges; AWS-managed ENIs in your subnet so endpoint control via SG rules; easier for compliance reviews because access is limited to a specific service endpoint.
- Cons: slightly higher egress path (hairpin through ENI) and cross-AZ hops in some configs. Throughput per ENI is finite; for large-scale bursts we shard endpoints across subnets/AZs.
- Operational checklist for pilot: create endpoint in a private subnet with 2 ENIs across AZs, add SG rule to allow 10.0.5.0/24 from app hosts, provide test mTLS certs, enable flow logs for troubleshooting.

2) VPC Peering
- Pros: minimal additional network hop and no ENI-level throughput limits; straight IP routing yields lowest RTT.
- Cons: cross-account peering requires explicit routes in both VPCs; you must be more deliberate about exposed CIDR ranges (less isolation). Also peering doesn't support transitive routing: if BlueCrest later wants to route through a third VPC, that becomes complex.
- Operational checklist: exchange peering request, update route tables (we recommend a PR review template), confirm no overlapping CIDRs, enable VPC flow logs.

3) Site-to-Site VPN
- Pros: quick for on-prem or when customers prefer a single IPSec tunnel.
- Cons: higher latency variance; not recommended for production inference traffic unless backed by dedicated appliances and active-active tunnels.
- Operational checklist: define IKE policies, BGP or static routes, MTU tuning, and monitoring / keepalives. We usually recommend BGP for automatic failover.

Performance expectations (ballpark, same-region):
- PrivateLink: additional 3–15ms p50 compared to peering depending on AZ layout and ENI placement.
- Peering: baseline minimal added latency, best p50.
- VPN: +20–80ms and higher jitter.

Security/Compliance: PrivateLink gives a clean audit story (endpoint + SGs + mTLS). Peering requires more careful CIDR hygiene but is doable for SOC2 customers with an approved architecture. VPNs often trigger network team reviews for cipher and logging.

Recommendation: Proceed with PrivateLink for the 3-week pilot. If p50 latency is within your SLA, we stay there and instrument cost/perf curves. If not, schedule a 48–72 hour peering POC during week 2 to compare. I'll help run the peering POC if needed.

-Karthik
Karthik Iyer
Principal Solutions Architect | Redwood Inference

Alex — circling back with a consolidated plan and attachments.

Decision: start pilot on PrivateLink (interface endpoint) to minimize friction and provide a clear security boundary. If during the pilot we see p50 latency >60ms or sustained throughput issues, we'll run a short peering POC in week 2.

Attached: mutual-action-plan-v2.pdf (MAP) — contains owner checklist, required subnets and SG rules.
Attached: bluecrest-mup-vpn-diagram.png — reference diagram for the VPN fallback (for NetOps).

Quick MAP highlights (from the PDF):
- BlueCrest: create PrivateLink interface endpoint in subnet us-west-2a/2b, allow outbound to 10.2.10.0/24, provide test token and three app hosts for smoke runs. (Owner: Alex)
- Redwood: whitelist endpoint ENI subnets on our side, provision test certs, and run synthetic latency tests during low-traffic windows. (Owner: Tessa/Karthik)
- Timing: endpoint and SG provisioning — day 0–1; validation + smoke runs — day 2–3; analysis & decide peering POC — day 7.
